newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: HIGH COURT DECISION ON REVENUE RAISING CAUSES CONFUSION
The states and territories are expected to announce an agreement with the Federal Government this afternoon over changes to their ability to raise revenue.
The High Court has ruled the states can only levy charges on tobacco, alcohol and petrol at rates of around six percent.
They currently raise about A$5 billion in revenue from the charges.
ACT Chief Minister Kate Carnell said an announcement will be made later today on how the Commonwealth intends to deal with the ruling.
"We've been having discussions with the Commonwealth on this issue for quite a while now because it was certainly indicated that the decision might come down the way that it did," Mrs Carnell said.

"I believe that by later on today we'll have an agreement in place with the Commonwealth that will ensure that there'll be no overall reduction in state or territory revenue, and little change to prices in the tobacco, liquor or petroleum product areas."
Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said the Commonwealth is ready to levy excise for the states and territories in the wake of the ruling.
Meanwhile, the anti-smoking lobby said the High Court decision is a victory for public health.
The chairman for Action on Smoking and Health Professor Simon Chapman said a centralised tax on tobacco will stop price discounting on cigarettes, which makes smoking more attractive to the young.

"Queensland in the past has had much lower tax rates than any of the other states and this has resulted in a lot of uneveness of tax around the country - bootlegging, price discounting and so forth," he said.
"If cigarettes are all going to be taxed at the same price, because they're going to be controlled centrally, I think we're going to be in for a much better era of tobacco control."
But Mr Costello said the Commonwealth will not tolerate state and territory governments attempting to use the decision to increase their revenue.

"We would say to those states which have lower than the uniform excise currently that the excess revenue should be returned to the wholesalers so that the wholesalers are reimbursed and prices don't rise," he said.
"One of the bottomlines as far as the Commonwealth is concerned is that we will not be a party to anything that puts up prices."
And the Institute of Chartered Accountants reacted to the decision by saying it emphasised the need for the Federal Government to take the lead on tax reform.
The executive director of the Institute of Chartered Accountants Stephen Harrison said the ruling means the Government has to quickly implement a stop-gap measure to protect dwindling state revenues.
GOVERNMENT WARNED NOT TO MISS I-T BOAT
It is claimed 100,000 jobs could be created nationwide, within five years, if the Federal Government took a more active approach to developing Australia's information technology exports.

Professor Ashley Goldsworthy, chair of the Federal IT Task Force, said countries such as the United States and Ireland have created thousands of jobs by recognising the importance of the information technology industry.
Professor Goldsworthy said their governments have offered big incentives and removed barriers to lure investors and generate employment.

South Australia's Information and Contract Services Minister Dean Brown said the Federal Government should develop a national framework for the development of the IT industry, or risk missing out further on jobs growth.
"Australia is in real danger of missing out on the...tens of thousands of jobs in information technology," Mr Brown said.
"We've become a major net importer of information technology, whereas we have the potential to become a major supplier to the rest of the world, particularly for Asia."
PROBE INTO QUEENSLAND CORRUPTION WATCHDOG SHUT DOWN BY COURT

The Supreme Court in Brisbane has terminated the multi-million dollar Connolly-Ryan Inquiry into the operations of Queensland's corruption watchdog, the Criminal Justice Commission (CJC), on the grounds of bias.

The State Government set up the inquiry late last year to look into the powers and functions of the CJC, including its investigation into a Police Union memorandum of understanding with the Coalition before the Mundingburra election.
That election led to the establishment of a Coalition government in the state.
The CJC, its chief investigator Mark Le Grand and former inquiry head Ken Carruthers took court action against commissioners Peter Connolly and Kevin Ryan to stop them from handing down their report.
In a week-long trial it was argued that inquiry was biased against them.
In a 96 page judgement, Justice Thomas agreed, ruling there is a strong case of ostensible bias on Mr Connolly's part.
He said there was a perception Mr Connolly favoured one side of politics.

In relation to Dr Ryan, Justice Thomas said he lacked the power and authority to complete the work of the inquiry and even if he had, it was unacceptable that he do so because of his extensive association with Mr Connolly.
Justice Thomas said the association was too great and it was too difficult to undo the influence.
Justice Thomas said the defence of immunity and waiver raised by the inquiry's lawyers should be rejected, and the injunction should be effective immediately.
As a result, the Connolly-Ryan Inquiry is to be shut down immediately, after having run for nine months, taken evidence from hundreds of people and cost more than A$11 million.
The CJC and Connolly Ryan Inquiry Commissioners have refused to comment on the ruling.
A spokeswoman for the commissioners said it is up to the Attorney General to decide whether to appeal against Justice James Thomas' judgement.
OPPOSITION WELCOMES DOWNER'S ATTACK ON HANSON
Attacks on Asian immigration by independent MP Pauline Hanson have had an alarming impact on Australia's reputation in the region, the Federal Opposition said today.
The Deputy Opposition Leader, Gareth Evans, welcomed criticisms of Ms Hanson made in Singapore by the Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer.
Mr Evans said the fall in Asian student enrolments in Australia and his own recent travels in Asia showed an alarming response to Ms Hanson.
"The old stereotypes about Australia being paternalistic, racist are coming out in droves," he said.
"It needs very, very strong and decisive action right across the board from the government, starting at the top."
CHARGES DISMISSED AGAINST MAN ACCUSED OF POLICEWOMAN ASSAULT
An ACT Magistrate has dismissed charges against a Brisbane man accused of seriously assaulting a female police officer.
Wayne Warton earlier pleaded not guilty to a number of assault charges.
It was alleged that on August 20 last year Mr Walton and another man repeatedly kicked and punched the officer during a rally outside Parliament House.
Magistrate Peter Dingwall dismissed the charges because of insufficient evidence.
The other man accused of the assault is still before the court.
